# R1 Digest — Introduction I–VII (940–1236)
**Coverage:** Full slice `R1_intro_940-1236.txt` (Introduction I–VII: Textual Criticism; Literary and Historical Criticism; Discourse Structure; Literary Structure and Message; Exegesis and Theology; Themes and Theology; Purpose of 2 Samuel). Outline and Bibliography excluded (not in file). Verbatim-anchored extraction only; attributed to David Toshio Tsumura (NICOT 2 Samuel Introduction).

## Claims

### C-R1-01 | DSS Samuel scrolls late publication and open questions
- **Claim (attributed Tsumura):** Although 4QSama, 4QSamb, and 4QSamc have been partly studied since 1952, they were not fully public until 1991 (facsimile) and 1993 (Brill microfiche); Cross et al.’s detailed DJD study appeared only in 2005. Open questions remain whether the three fragment groups constitute three independent scrolls (4QSamb and especially 4QSamc being very fragmentary), and whether 4QSama is a biblical manuscript or a midrashic document (Kratz).
- **Quote:** "whether 4QSama was a biblical manuscript (Bibelhandschrift) or a midrashic document"
- **Locus:** I.A Method of Textual Reconstruction in DJD (2005)
- **Targets:** [[2-samuel]], [[tsumura-2-samuel-nicot]], [[1-samuel]]

### C-R1-02 | Critique of Cross/DJD reconstruction vs Herbert’s objective criteria
- **Claim (attributed Tsumura):** Cross and Parry’s DJD reconstructions use ad hoc spacing remarks (“spacing requires,” “no room,” etc.), whereas E. D. Herbert provides more objective criteria (average column widths and average letter widths). Despite Herbert’s contributions, Cross’s school ignored them in DJD. E.g., DJD (like McCarter) reconstructs hʾlwhym after ḥesed in 2 Sam. 2:5 as a MT–LXXA conflation, but Herbert had shown the insertion “unlikely” (reconstructed width 11% above section-a average). In 2 Sam. 21:5 McCarter/Cross et al. prefer LXX-based klh ʿlynw wyrdpnw and dmh lhšmydnw over MT; Herbert holds those reconstructions do not fit 4QSama lacunae (would exceed ACW maxima). Fincke’s handwritten reconstruction misleadingly shortens a line calculated at 117.71 mm.
- **Quote:** "Cross and his school ignored it in their most recent study in DJD"
- **Locus:** I.A Method of Textual Reconstruction in DJD (2005); examples 2 Sam. 2:5; 21:5
- **Targets:** [[2-samuel]], [[tsumura-2-samuel-nicot]]

### C-R1-03 | MT, LXX, and DSS relationships are not one-sided
- **Claim (attributed Tsumura):** Against R. W. Klein’s RBL (Dec. 2007) claim that Tsumura ignored LXX readings confirmed by Cave 4 Samuel manuscripts as alternate Hebrew Vorlage: that is only one side of the fact. Sometimes MT is supported by DSS against LXX (e.g. 2 Sam. 3:28-29, 14:26); sometimes MT by LXX against 4QSama (e.g. 5:6); both LXXBAL and 4QSama wrongly supply “Mephibosheth” before MT “son of Saul” in 4:1; at 6:17 MT+LXX supported by 4QSama yet McCarter would omit as “secondary.” Details deferred to passage comments.
- **Quote:** "this is just one side of \"the fact.\""
- **Locus:** I.B Relationship among MT, LXX, and DSS
- **Targets:** [[2-samuel]], [[tsumura-2-samuel-nicot]], [[tsumura-1-samuel-nicot]]

### C-R1-04 | Phonetic spelling as alternative to corruption theory
- **Claim (attributed Tsumura):** Some MT readings usually labeled “corrupt” are “phonetic spellings,” reflecting phonetic reality behind scripts rather than formal scribal dittography/haplography. Ugaritic misspellings (vowel sandhi; loss of ʾ, r, l, m, n; addition of q, etc.) show scribes write phonetic reality into text. E.g., Bedan (1 Sam. 12:11) may be phonetic realization of Baraq rather than corruption. Such “corrupt” MT readings are often lectio difficilior and thus more original by traditional criteria; phonetic spellings in 1–2 Samuel are more than “few forms” (contra Klein) and often argue against scribal-error theory. Lists many 1 Sam. and 2 Sam. verses where phonetic spellings appear (2 Sam. includes 3:1, 8; 4:6; 5:2, 13; 7:7; 8:8; 11:24; 13:16; 14:19; 18:3, 12; 19:13; 20:5, 9, 14; 21:9, 12, 16; 22:6, 8, 27, 36, 40, 46; 23:8, 9, 20, 21, 29, 31, etc.).
- **Quote:** "some MT readings usually considered \"corrupt\" are in fact not corruptions but \"phonetic spellings.\""
- **Locus:** I.C “Phonetic Spelling” — The Phonetic Reality Behind the Scripts
- **Targets:** [[2-samuel]], [[1-samuel]], [[tsumura-2-samuel-nicot]], [[tsumura-1-samuel-nicot]]

### C-R1-05 | Synchronic priority before diachronic reconstruction
- **Claim (attributed Tsumura):** Any theory of literary composition must rest on literary and linguistic reading of the text itself. A diachronic approach should be preceded by synchronic study “as it is”: note variants and discrepancies first, then go behind the text. Both traditional historical-critical (diachronic-only) and recent synchronic-only intertextuality approaches ignore this principle. Saussure distinguished synchronic/diachronic and put priority on synchronic without eliminating history; recent synchronic-only emphasis is an overreaction that can discard the spatio-temporal (historical) approach.
- **Quote:** "a diachronic approach to a biblical text should be preceded by a synchronic study of the text as it is"
- **Locus:** II.A Principle of Synchronic Priority
- **Targets:** [[2-samuel]], [[1-samuel]], [[tsumura-2-samuel-nicot]], [[david-tsumura]]

### C-R1-06 | Critique of intertextuality / postmodern narrative criticism (Lyke)
- **Claim (attributed Tsumura):** Synchronic-only literary approach is exemplified by intertextuality emphasis (e.g. L. L. Lyke on the wise woman of Tekoa, 2 Sam. 14, via Stern’s midrashic meshalim and Bakhtin’s “dialogization”). Criticisms: (1) assuming multivocal/polysemous quality from “multiple voices” is tautological—mashal meaning is fixed by particular context; distinguish author’s intended ambiguity from postmodern inability to decide; avoid word-association games; (2) narrow elements (“two sons”) appear across ANE wisdom; narrowing element + broadening context risks level-skipping and ignoring immediate context; limited ANE evidence may cause modern indeterminacy rather than authorial design; (3) for comparison, difference matters more than similarity; overemphasizing similarities is disastrous—need competence to read biblical mashal in original ANE cultural-historical setting and notice uniqueness.
- **Quote:** "An overemphasis on similarities is disastrous to intertextual study."
- **Locus:** II.B Intertextuality
- **Targets:** [[2-samuel]], [[david]], [[tsumura-2-samuel-nicot]]

### C-R1-07 | Minor characters subordinate to major figures and God’s plan
- **Claim (attributed Tsumura):** New literary criticism’s focus on characters/characterization (Simon on minor characters; studies of Eliab, Joab, Abigail, etc.) can disclose biblical views of human complexity, but the author/narrator treats minor characters mainly in relation to major characters (David, Saul, Samuel). Jonathan opposes Saul in relation to David; Amnon–Tamar (13:1-22) sits in Absalom’s revolt (13:1–20:26) and ultimately around David–Absalom; Joab’s significance is via masters David then Solomon. 1–2 Samuel is not a collection of stories about dramatis personae, nor even worthy of being called David’s biography. Concern is how God, Lord of history, guides history through human agents so divine purpose of saving his people may be fulfilled through the messiah king at Zion (e.g. Ps. 132). Character studies profitable when controlled by spatio-temporal cultural/historical reality.
- **Quote:** "Even a part of 1–2 Samuel is not worthy to be called David's biography."
- **Locus:** II.C Characters and Characterizations
- **Targets:** [[2-samuel]], [[1-samuel]], [[david]], [[tsumura-2-samuel-nicot]]

### C-R1-08 | Date and authorship: early divided monarchy (Rehoboam / late 10th c.)
- **Claim (attributed Tsumura):** Final editors of 1–2 Samuel “probably worked around a time not later than the late tenth century, that is, the early period of Rehoboam’s reign,” in light of 1 Sam. 27:6 (“Ziklag has belonged to the kings of Judah to this day”). Halpern: Negev picture in Samuel fits 10th-century evidence not later; Shishaq (925 B.C.) connection places 2 Samuel no later than 9th century reflecting 10th-century memories; 1 Sam. 27:6 unlikely even for ninth century after Shishaq. Large parts of United Monarchy information (2 Sam. 8) from roughly contemporary sources (Halpern). Eternal dynasty/kingship in 2 Sam. 7 not late—parallels in Ugaritic Baal Cycle (KTU 1.2 IV 10) and Alashia letter RS 18.113A+B; Laato: Assyrian royal building inscriptions support eternal dynasty idea in Israelite royal ideology already when David planned the Temple—supports 2 Sam. 7 from united monarchy era. Opinion from prior volume still holds: composed earliest period of divided monarchy, possibly slightly modernized in ninth century. Official history of dynasty founder reasonably written third generation—Rehoboam, tenth century.
- **Quote:** "1–2 Samuel was composed during the earliest period of the divided monarchy still holds"
- **Locus:** II.D Date and Authorship
- **Targets:** [[2-samuel]], [[1-samuel]], [[davidic-covenant]], [[david]], [[tsumura-2-samuel-nicot]], [[tsumura-1-samuel-nicot]]

### C-R1-09 | Genre: intermediate between epic (Judges) and annalistic (Kings); DH skepticism
- **Claim (attributed Tsumura):** Noth’s Deuteronomistic history (DH) / DTR remains influential but one must ask what kind of history/narrative Samuel is—genre cannot be ignored. Judges–Kings may all be narrative prose, yet stylistically Judges is more epic, Kings annalistic, Samuel intermediate with both epic and annalistic features. Vs Chronicles, Samuel is less annalistic history than epic-like story (e.g. David eighth son in 1 Sam. 16 vs seventh in 1 Chr. 2:15; Canaanite x // x+1 number parallelism allows seventh-and-eighth description). Saul’s reign: narrator ignores age/length (1 Sam. 13:1), describing only two years (smallest BH numeral) as already rejected—annalistic Kings would care about accession age and exact reign; Judges uses round numbers for judges. Macrostructure-only narrative critics (and DH-driven holistic Joshua–2 Kings historiography) ignore genre uniqueness of individual books; time to attend uniqueness of Judges, Samuel, Kings rather than universal aspects of the whole.
- **Quote:** "Samuel is in an intermediate position, exhibiting both epic elements and annalistic features."
- **Locus:** II.E Genre and Style
- **Targets:** [[2-samuel]], [[1-samuel]], [[david]], [[tsumura-2-samuel-nicot]]

### C-R1-10 | Discourse grammar: wayqtl initial vs sequential; SETTING/TERMINUS; weqtl procedural
- **Claim (attributed Tsumura):** Discourse grammar concerns how sentence structure/forms guide discourse (cf. vol. 1). Longacre: verb-initial wayqtl normally main-line, but not every wayqtl is main-line. Distinctions: (1) every wayqtl with stated subject initiates a new discourse unit (subparagraph)—waw is initial; wayqtl without stated subject within subparagraph carries previous EVENT—waw sequential; (2) wayqtl can appear in SETTING (impersonal subject e.g. 11:27; 24:1, 4; plural with non–dramatis persona) or TRANSITION (movement verbs e.g. 4:5; 12:1) rather than EVENT; (3) weqtl after wayqtl sequence is PROCEDURAL discourse (HOW) vs NARRATIVE (WHAT)—e.g. 2 Sam. 7; (4) Hebrew dialogue pattern: A to B / He says / He says / B says to A—fourth speaker normally specified; 2 Sam. 18:23 needs “And he said” supplied by this pattern.
- **Quote:** "in the former the verbal form weqtl describes HOW it happens (e.g., 2 Sam. 7)."
- **Locus:** III. Discourse Structure (1–4)
- **Targets:** [[2-samuel]], [[davidic-covenant]], [[tsumura-2-samuel-nicot]], [[tsumura-1-samuel-nicot]]

### C-R1-11 | Literary structure of 1–2 Samuel (Prologue through Epilogues)
- **Claim (attributed Tsumura):** Structure of 1–2 Samuel: I. Prologue (1 Sam. 1:1–7:17) Story of Samuel with embedded Story of the Ark; II. Transition to Monarchy (1 Sam. 8); III. Story of Saul (1 Sam. 9:1–15:35); IV. Story of Saul and David (1 Sam. 16:1–31:13); V. Story of King David (2 Sam. 1:1–20:26) comprising (i) Story of David’s Reign (1:1–12:31) with units A Death of Saul; B King David; C Jerusalem City of David; D Zion Place of Worship; E Davidic Covenant Eternal Throne; F Catalogue of Military Activities; G Mephibosheth; H Israel-Ammon War framed as 1,[A] beginning / 2,[X] David and Bathsheba / 3,[B] end; (ii) Story of Absalom’s Revolt (13:1–20:26) A Absalom the Rebel; B Absalom’s Rebellion; C David’s Officers; VI. Epilogues (2 Sam. 21:1–24:25).
- **Quote:** "V. \"Story of King David\" (2 Sam. 1:1–20:26)"
- **Locus:** IV.A The Literary Structure of 1–2 Samuel
- **Targets:** [[2-samuel]], [[1-samuel]], [[david]], [[davidic-covenant]], [[tsumura-2-samuel-nicot]]

### C-R1-12 | Epilogues concentric ABXX′B′A′ structure
- **Claim (attributed Tsumura):** Epilogues (2 Sam. 21:1–24:25) form concentric structure: A Famine and Death of Saul’s Sons (21:1-14); B Philistine War (21:15-22); X Song of David (22:1-51) = Ps. 18; X′ Last Words of David (23:1-7); B′ David’s Heroes (23:8-39); A′ Census and the Lord’s Anger (24:1-25).
- **Quote:** "X. Song of David (22:1-51) = Ps. 18" / "X′. Last Words of David (23:1-7)"
- **Locus:** IV.A VI. Epilogues (2 Sam. 21:1–24:25)
- **Targets:** [[2-samuel]], [[david]], [[tsumura-2-samuel-nicot]]

### C-R1-13 | Message: divine sovereignty, human institutions, providential guidance
- **Claim (attributed Tsumura):** Message is built into literary structure. Message of 1–2 Samuel: how Yahweh, Lord of history, through human institution of monarchy guides his covenant people providentially by gracious and sovereign hands. Main concerns: relationship between divine sovereignty and human institutions; between God’s providential guidance and human responsibility. Rom. 8:28 summarizes divine dealings with covenant people. Books are not biography of particular persons, not even of King David; minor-character emphasis may help complex personality of David as human messiah but may mislead into nonsubstantial themes. Historical narrative of God’s salvation history advancing divine plan, including one big step in the Davidic covenant, eventually fulfilled in Jesus Christ, heir of David (Matt. 1:1). Despite David’s serious failures, Yahweh works his plan, establishing grace and faithfulness (Ps. 89) regardless of people’s faithlessness.
- **Quote:** "how Yahweh, the Lord of history, through the human institution of monarchy guides his covenant people providentially"
- **Locus:** IV.B The Message of 1–2 Samuel
- **Targets:** [[2-samuel]], [[1-samuel]], [[david]], [[davidic-covenant]], [[tsumura-2-samuel-nicot]]

### C-R1-14 | Theme: Human Desires and Divine Plans (Hannah, Saul, David)
- **Claim (attributed Tsumura):** One theme running through 1–2 Samuel is human desires and divine plans. (i) Hannah desired a boy and vowed dedication; God made her mother of the king-maker, greater than expected. (ii) Saul did not start desiring kingship but exerted himself to meet people’s expectation (“longing of all Israel” 1 Sam. 9:20), concerned with people’s opinion rather than Lord’s will; fearing people, neglected fearing Lord (chs. 13, 15). (iii) David desired to build a house for the Lord; Lord refused (2 Sam. 7)—God’s plan was eternal Davidic throne (7:16). Chronicles (1 Chr. 22:8; 28:3) explains refusal by wars/bloodshed; through David’s census sin (2 Sam. 24) God led purchase of Araunah’s threshing floor where Solomon later built the temple. God’s plan of salvation continues despite phases of human desire; God proceeds by holy sovereignty and grace.
- **Quote:** "One theme that runs through 1–2 Samuel is that of human desires and divine plans."
- **Locus:** IV.B Human Desires and Divine Plans
- **Targets:** [[2-samuel]], [[1-samuel]], [[david]], [[davidic-covenant]], [[tsumura-2-samuel-nicot]]

### C-R1-15 | Defense of historical-grammatical exegesis vs Chapman’s literary critique
- **Claim (attributed Tsumura):** Critics (e.g. S. Chapman) said 1 Samuel commentary lacked theological depth and ignored narrative literary contours, alleging “fatal” presumptions that history is primary bearer of theological significance and that Samuel is read for history-likeness, streamlining subtlety. Tsumura: Chapman’s subjective literary approach reads into narrative what is not there—e.g. treating Saul’s seven-day wait at Gilgal (1 Sam. 13:8) as “narrative forgetting” device to increase sympathy with Saul. Synchronically, Saul went to Gilgal more than once (official installation 11:15); seven-day ritual waiting is common ANE religio-cultural practice. Exegete needs to read text as it is with ANE common sense. Grammar shapes meaning (e.g. ʿal “against”/“on” in 2 Sam. 14:1; ʾappāyim in 1 Sam. 1:5). Theological understanding of 2 Sam. 7 depends on grammatical analysis: weqtl tense in 9b-11b vs 18b-19 as “poetic prose”; speaker-oriented ʿal-kēn and vertical grammar AXX′B in v. 22; crux in v. 23; two senses of *pdh via Ugaritic economic texts.
- **Quote:** "Chapman's subjective literary narrative approach is reading into the narrative what is not there."
- **Locus:** V. Exegesis and Theology
- **Targets:** [[2-samuel]], [[1-samuel]], [[davidic-covenant]], [[tsumura-2-samuel-nicot]], [[tsumura-1-samuel-nicot]], [[david-tsumura]]

### C-R1-16 | Themes: David’s throne and heir; prophetic and NT trajectory
- **Claim (attributed Tsumura):** Two important themes in 2 Samuel are David’s throne and his heir, especially in Yahweh’s promise in 2 Sam. 7, as also in Ps. 89:4 (29, 36) zeraʿ and kissēʾ; Ps. 132 dual elections of heir (v. 11; cf. 2 Sam. 7) and Zion (v. 13; cf. 2 Sam. 6). Throne theme continues in prophetic literature (kissēʾ Dāwīd Isa. 9:7); heir theme as branch ṣemaḥ (Isa. 4:2; Jer. 23:5; 33:15; Zech. 3:8; 6:12), shoot/sprout (Isa. 11:1; cf. Rev. 5:5; 22:16). Messianically “house of David” carries both themes (Luke 1:32 throne; 1:69 house).
- **Quote:** "Two important themes in 2 Samuel are David's throne and his heir"
- **Locus:** VI.A David’s Throne and His Heir
- **Targets:** [[2-samuel]], [[david]], [[davidic-covenant]], [[tsumura-2-samuel-nicot]]

### C-R1-17 | Davidic covenant as central theme of 2 Samuel and OT salvation plan
- **Claim (attributed Tsumura):** Davidic covenant (2 Sam. 7) is the central theme of 2 Samuel, even of the entire Old Testament—a turning point in the divine plan of salvation, reflected in Matt. 1:1 placing David midpoint between Abraham and Jesus. Lord promises David a dynasty (house, v. 11b), raising offspring and establishing eternal kingdom and throne (vv. 12-13) so David’s throne established forever (v. 16); fulfilled in Jesus the Messiah (Luke 1:33). Theology of 2 Samuel: God’s character in dealings with people, especially chosen individuals, with grace (ḥesed) for his plan; faithful to Abrahamic promise (Gen. 12:1-3), graciously deals with David so salvation plan further fulfilled and completed in Jesus Christ the Messiah (2 Sam. 7:11b-16).
- **Quote:** "the Davidic covenant (2 Sam. 7) is the central theme of 2 Samuel, even of the entire Old Testament."
- **Locus:** VI.B Davidic Covenant
- **Targets:** [[davidic-covenant]], [[2-samuel]], [[david]], [[tsumura-2-samuel-nicot]]

### C-R1-18 | Purpose of 2 Samuel (continuity with 1 Samuel; eternal covenant; temple hint)
- **Claim (attributed Tsumura):** Purpose of 1 Samuel was twofold: (1) explain meaning of establishment of monarchy in Israel; (2) show how Lord prepared David to sit on throne after Saul. First purpose continues. Purpose of 2 Samuel: not only explain Israelite monarchy as political institution but show how God led King David’s life specifically despite grave sins against God in order to keep his promise to provide heirs—finally the heir—to establish his eternal dynasty. Ch. 7: prototype messiah granted promise that kingdom and heir’s throne established forever; with Davidic covenant, salvation plan moves a big step since Abraham a thousand years earlier. Last words (23:2-7) near book’s end reference “eternal covenant” (berît ʿôlām) God made with David (v. 5); because of this covenant of faithfulness/grace (ḥesed), Jesus the Messiah died sacrificially for human sin. Ch. 24 points to place of worship where David’s son would build temple for true King at Zion/Jerusalem; as monarchy sidetracked people from true King, Solomon’s Temple would lead people to physical temple away from real presence of God. Salvation = recovery of fellowship with holy God; humans created as image for (1) worship Creator (2) rule as vice-regent (Gen. 1:26-27); true recovery in true Messiah. 1–2 Samuel ends hinting preparation for temple worship as prototype of true worship through Jesus Christ, true Messiah.
- **Quote:** "how God led King David's life specifically despite his grave sins against God in order to keep his promise to provide heirs"
- **Locus:** VII. Purpose of 2 Samuel
- **Targets:** [[2-samuel]], [[1-samuel]], [[david]], [[davidic-covenant]], [[tsumura-2-samuel-nicot]], [[tsumura-1-samuel-nicot]]
